title: A year of a household's electric bills and what changed
summary: A fictional year separates electricity use from a midyear rate increase.

blocks.heading: The bill rose 10.5%; usage did not
blocks.body: This invented household used 10,500 kWh. A July increase in the energy rate from $0.12 to $0.15/kWh added $153 compared with keeping the old rate all year. This example excludes taxes and other charges; each month has a $16 fixed charge.

blocks.heading: All twelve bills
blocks.caption: Bill = $16 + kWh × rate. First-half use: 5,400 kWh. Second-half use: 5,100 kWh.

blocks.heading: Compare against the right baseline
blocks.body: Actual annual cost is $1,605. Keeping $0.12/kWh all year would cost $1,452 for exactly the same usage. The $153 difference is price, not additional consumption. Summer peaks are visible, but these numbers alone do not prove air conditioning caused them.

blocks.heading: The next useful evidence
blocks.body: Compare kWh per day with the same months of the prior year and weather. Note billing-period length, estimated readings and new appliances. A dollars-only chart would mix together rate changes and household behavior.
